description: Looking for someone who can contribute to creating a space-exploring app
summary: Outpost Commander is a space-base survival game where a child commands 4 astronauts while the environment changes using real NASA space weather data. They need to pack a rocket with sun panels, nuclear battery, big batteries, and soil roof, then assign jobs to other astronauts (like science, plants, building the roof, and cleaning panels) across a 10-day or 30-day mission. The crew must shelter or keep working to survive till the mission ends.
details:
Outpost Commander is a browser game where a child commands a four-astronaut space base. Players pack a space rocket with sun panels, a nuclear battery, big batteries, and soil roofs. Each mission day they give every astronaut a job (science, plants, building the roof, or cleaning panels), and they balance power, air, food, and space rays. Every mission day replays a real day of those planets, like solar flares from NASA’s DONKI database from the last 30 days. The flare class sets the radiation dose, and when a flare hits, the player must decide whether to shelter the crew or keep working. Every choice has a trade-off: sheltering protects the crew but costs a whole workday, and extra science drains power. Missions run for 10 or 30 days and end with a star rating and feedback report. If NASA can’t be reached, the game switches to a clearly labeled "practice mode” with simulated flares, so it never passes off static data as live.

The game helps children learn real space weather, radiation safety, and resource management by playing. Kid-friendly language, a guided onboarding flow, and “Did you know?” tips explain concepts such as why soil and rock block radiation. Adults can learn alongside them. We hope it makes the dangers of life beyond Earth feel real, builds interest in space science, and shows that real NASA data can be turned into something young people want to play. It runs free in any modern browser on phones, tablets, and computers, so classrooms and families can use it without special hardware.

We built it in TypeScript throughout: React 18 and Vite 5 for the interface (with HTML and CSS for the dark space theme, animations, and responsive layout), and Node.js with NestJS 10 for a small API that fetches DONKI flare data and caches it for one hour to avoid rate limits. The game engine is plain TypeScript, so the rules can be unit tested on their own and scaled to 10-day and 30-day missions. The API has Swagger/OpenAPI docs, the code lives in one GitHub repository using npm workspaces, and the live site is hosted on Vercel. We made the video in Canva and used the Nunito font. Standard laptops were all we needed. The project is creative because it turns a real NASA feed into a playable story: each day’s danger is a real flare from the past month, so no two missions feel the same. In designing it, we considered honesty about data, kid-friendly wording, mobile layouts, API reliability, and keeping the rules fun but trade-off-driven.
